subject: africanElephant
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: adult African bush elephant.
Style: low-poly.
reasoning:
I need to design a full module for a low-poly African bush elephant, including skeleton, rig, and textures, while being careful with the SDK API since I can't test it directly. I'm working out realistic proportions—around 3.2m shoulder height, 6m body length including trunk, and 1.5m tusks—to guide the build.

Now I'm mapping out the skeleton hierarchy: hip root position, a spine chain running from rump to shoulder using catmull-spline joints, a head joint with a large skull sphere and forehead dome, and the trunk extending from the face down to the ground. I'm working through the exact joint coordinates and naming so the parent-child relationships between hips and spine segments make sense.

Continuing the trunk curling forward with a tapering radius, then setting up the tail chain from the hips with three joints ending in a tuft, before moving to the four legs positioned at their x-offsets.

Now I'm working out the leg geometry with columnar elephant-style segments, placing shoulder and foot targets then solving segment lengths and bend angles so the reach matches the actual root-to-foot distance.

For the hind leg I'm setting bend directions so the knee goes forward and the hock curves back, matching an elephant's gait. I'm defining the leg as a tapered tube with radius shrinking from thigh to lower leg, then widening slightly at the ankle, topped off with a wide flat foot cylinder and a few small pale toenail boxes near the front.

Now I'm thinking about the body shape, considering lofting it along the spine path using station widths and heights, possibly tying the loft to the spine and hip bone chain or sweeping an elliptical radius profile along the neck-to-spine path instead.

Working through the body stations from rump to shoulders, I'm adjusting the center height, width, and depth at each z-position to get the elephant's characteristic profile -- dipping back and rising shoulders -- while keeping the top around 3.2-3.3 units for realistic shoulder height.

Continuing the station at z=1.65 where neck and chest merge, then I'm checking how the loft function handles end caps and whether it accepts a bone chain or list of joints for skinning.

So instead I'll keep hips as root and offset the spine chain's starting joint slightly forward of it, with spine1, spine2, and chest positioned along the path up to the chest—accepting that spine1 isn't exactly the pelvis but staying parented correctly to hips.

Now I'm thinking through the ears: African elephant ears are huge, roughly 1.2m, so I need to extrude an outlined ear shape with the drawing in the side (Y-Z) plane and thickness running along X, so it sits flat against the head but flares outward.

Still working out ear geometry...

Closing the polygon confirms a simple, non-self-intersecting clockwise shape with slight smoothing and thin extrusion. I'm adding a hinge joint for rigging at the ear's attachment point, aimed backward-outward, and planning the ear's paint with a mottled gray base, pinker gradient near the lower edge, and a darker rim.

Now I'm shaping the head: a skull sphere scaled for width/height/depth, a forehead dome layered above it, cheek bulges on the sides, and a muzzle frustum at the front leading into a trunk base. I'm sketching the trunk as a thick tapering sweep starting from the face and curving downward and forward, setting up joint points along its path for articulation.

Continuing to plot the trunk's curve, I want it to hang naturally but curl slightly upward at the tip for some charm, keeping the lowest point just above the ground. I'm defining the taper radii at each section and using a simple low-poly octagonal cross-section for the trunk segments.

I'll use flat shading on the trunk and legs to keep that faceted, low-poly feel, then add subtle wrinkle rings along the trunk using thin torus shapes aligned to the sweep path's tangent at intervals.

Still working out the ring radius...

Actually, I'm reconsidering—maybe stripe-based paint shading for bark ridges along the trunk is simpler and cheaper than placing many tori, though the tori give a nicer low-poly silhouette, so I'll try a modest combination of sparse tori plus painted ridge bands.

For skin color, I'm defining a shared elephant gray-brown palette with dusty red-brown tones near the legs, using noise to blend wrinkle patches and dust gradients by height, plus small cell-based cracks for dry skin texture—keeping one `SKIN` paint function reused across all body parts for visual continuity.

Now I'm planning the decal textures (aiming for 5-12 total): first up is an EYE texture—small amber iris with black pupil, dark wrinkle outline, and eyelid lashes, decaled onto the skull surface at a hit point using the surface/decal system. Next I'm sketching an EAR_VEIN texture for added surface detail.

Working out ear decal placement...

I figure out the outward direction by computing the sign of the axis dot product, then scale the ear axis vector by that sign to get the decal orientation. I consider placing veins on both the outer and inner faces using opposite directions, weighing the extra cost against keeping things simple given the small segment count.

Actually, decals seem riskier here, so I decide to switch to a paint-based approach instead: grey base color with a pink rim and lower tint, plus noise-driven vein ridges where the darker lines appear when the noise value is close to 0.5. This avoids needing a separate texture. I also start planning which other small textures to include, like tail-tuft hair strands and trunk-base bristle cards, to stay within the target texture count.

For the ear plane orientation, I need the +Z facing outward along the normal with up along +Y, but since the ear isn't rectangular, I'll clip the vein texture to the ear outline shape so it doesn't bleed past the edges.

I can reuse the same outline array to build the SVG viewBox, drawing the veins as thin dark strokes clipped to a slightly shrunk polygon so the smoothed 3D mesh doesn't show texture overhang at the edges. I'll size the plane to match the ear's bounding box and center it there, then figure out how the drawing's horizontal axis maps onto the mesh's orientation.

Working through the cross products for camera right-vectors, I confirm that for the left ear (s=1) viewed from outside, the drawing's unmirrored +u direction correctly lines up as "right" on screen, so no flip is needed there — but I still need to check the mirrored case for the right ear (s=-1).

Rather than fighting with negative scale and winding-order flips, which could cause export issues, I'm leaning toward just generating two separate vein textures, one for each ear, so I don't have to rely on mirroring logic at all.

Good, since the ear plane contains the Y axis exactly, the up vector works fine, so I can place the plane centered on the ear using local coordinates with the outline's x,y and thickness axis determining the front/back face positions.

I'm using the ear's facing axis as the thickness direction, determining which side is "outer" by checking its dot product with the side vector, then setting the outer face position and normal accordingly, with the inner face on the opposite side.

For texture orientation, I'm figuring out when each face needs mirroring based on viewer perspective: outer face on s=1 stays unmirrored, but on s=-1 it needs the mirrored texture, while the inner faces flip the opposite way. I simplify this by just checking the sign of the normal's x-component to pick between the left and right ear textures.

Now I'm checking the ear's attachment position and proportions against the head - the root sits near the shoulder, and I want the ear to be roughly 1.4 tall by 1.1 wide to match typical African elephant ear scale.

I'm also verifying that the ear doesn't clip into the body geometry at that z-position, computing the ear tip's x and z offsets using the tilted direction vector and comparing against the body's half-width at that cross-section.

Now I'm sketching the tusks as bezier curves sprouting from the upper jaw beside the trunk, defining base, control points, and tip positions so they curve forward-down then sweep outward, while making sure they clear the trunk's radius near the top.

For the tusk geometry, I'm tapering the radius from base to tip, adding a small dark collar ring at the base, and shading with an ivory-to-worn-brown gradient along the path. Then I'm positioning the eyes symmetrically on the sides of the skull near the brow area.

For the eye itself, I want something more realistic than a flat decal, so I'm making a small flattened dark sphere inset into the socket, adding a ring of thin lash spikes around it, and a subtle wedge above for the brow ridge. The jaw will be a separate joint so it can articulate independently from the skull.

Now building the lower jaw as a tapered frustum shape beneath the trunk, plus a small pink mouth-interior box tucked into the gap to suggest depth without overcomplicating the geometry.

Shifting to the skull and face: I'm placing a main skull sphere with flattened radii, positioning the muzzle base as a separate sphere/box that merges into the forehead, adding cheek bulges on either side, and topping it off with a dome sphere for the crown of the head.

Giving the elephant its characteristic twin-domed forehead by adding two small bumps near the top, attaching all head geometry to a head bone joint, then adding sparse hair tufts scattered across the forehead and trunk base using card textures, and starting on a segmented tail chain from the hips.

Working out the tail path with catmull-rom points down to a tapered tip, then placing a ring of hanging tuft cards at the end to give it a hairy tassel look.

I'll add a tail-tip base cylinder, then move to body wrinkle decals, applying them to the loft surface of the body as the decal target.

For wrinkles, I'm placing decals at specific directional hits around the body center, using a skin-fold texture with dark semi-transparent curved strokes. I'm also planning mud splatter decals on the belly and legs using a brownish blob texture, though I'm considering handling leg mud through gradient paint instead of decals.

Now I'm working out knee and ankle wrinkle rings, plus toenails as small ivory-grey boxes arranged around the front perimeter of each foot, oriented outward from the foot's center.

Front feet get 5 nails, hind feet get 4, placed in an arc and aimed outward along the foot's boundary, attached to the leg chain's tip bone.

Now I'm working out the IK limb placement for the front legs, checking root and target positions relative to the body so the shoulder joint sits inside the torso and the foot lands near the ground with appropriate segment lengths for a slight bend.

For the hind legs, I'm setting similar root/target coordinates further back, with the knee bending forward and the hock bending backward to mimic an elephant's gait. I'm also confirming the limb bends stay within the correct plane defined by root, target, and the hint vector, so vertically aligned joints don't create ambiguous bend directions.

Now I'm working out the tube sweep parameters for the legs — a tapering radius array along the chain, 8-sided cross-sections, and deciding whether to disable smoothing so the leg segments read as faceted rather than perfectly round.

I'm also checking the foot geometry: the leg's round end cap would dip the mesh below the floor, so I'm switching the leg caps to flat and enlarging the foot cylinder slightly so it still covers the leg's bottom edge without poking through.

Now I'm shading the feet with the same skin material gradient based on height, and adding a small torus around the ankle as a darker cuff detail to mark where the foot meets the leg.

I'm thinking through the texture resolution limits — with the elephant's large surface area, the baked texture density gives roughly 9mm texels, which means fine 5mm crack details in the skin won't actually resolve cleanly, so I need to widen the crack threshold to around 2cm to stay visible at this texture density.

I'll bump the paint size to 2048 for finer detail but keep the atlas manageable by using smaller textures elsewhere, and limit the palette to 64 flat colors overall. For richness I'm adding eyelashes as a ring of small spikes around the eye socket, oriented outward and arced across the upper lid.

I'm also sketching a brow ridge and considering a small dark tear-streak decal under the eye, possibly as its own tiny gradient texture rather than folding it into the eye texture.

Now I'm counting up my texture set (eye, stain, wrinkle, mud, tuft, bristle, and ear textures, eight total), and thinking through the trunk tip detail — adding a small nub and two flattened dark nostril discs on the end face, positioned using the trunk's tip frame orientation.

Placing the nostrils requires using a ring arrangement around the trunk's end axis so they land symmetrically on the left and right sides rather than top and bottom, which means tuning the angle range so items land at 90° and 270°. I need to account for the item frame's outward radial orientation when attaching the nostril spheres so they sit flush rather than sticking out sideways.

Adding dorsal finger details...

Now I'm setting up the trunk chain parented to the head, using five joints along a catmull-rom path with a tapering radius function for the sweep, treating it as a tentacle-type bone.

Then I'm detailing the head's skin anatomy: the skull sphere with painted skin material, a jaw joint aimed toward the mouth with a lower jaw frustum and lip parts, plus nails, toenails, and tusk coloring including the dark gum sheath at the tusk base.

I'm sketching extra surface details like chin bristles, shoulder wrinkle decals, lighter belly or dust accents, and sparse back bristle cards scattered over the upper body for texture. Now I'm starting to lay out the actual Three.js code structure for the model.

Setting up imports and paint color palette...

Adding wrinkles, dust, and mud texture layers...

I'm realizing the per-texel cell computation could be slow at 2048² resolution with 27 cells per sample, so I should consider reducing paint size or density to keep baking fast enough, estimating around 70m² of surface area across body, legs, head, and ears.

I'll reduce to three noise calls plus cells for efficiency, keeping default paint size of 1024. For the ear paint, I'm building it by sampling the skin's base color at each point and then blending toward pink near the rim using a smoothstep based on the outline value, darkening the edges for depth.

For the tusk paint, I'm blending between cream and tan tones with noise, shifting to a darker brown near the base and adding scuffed streaks toward the tip. I'll construct the tusk's path using a cubic bezier curve defined by four control points.

For the body, I'm thinking through the loft function's station-based approach, considering cross-section options like ngon segments versus a plain circle count, and leaning toward a flat-shaded polygon with around 10-12 sides for the low-poly look.

I also need to reconsider the bone list for the loft — since the torso stations extend past the spine chain into the neck region, I should include the neck chain in the bone list too, so the loft follows hips, spine, and neck together rather than just hips and spine.

Rest pose vertex positions stay unaffected by weighting, so this shouldn't cause skinning issues. I'll set hips at [0,2.4,-1.3], parent front legs to the chest joint at the spine tip, and parent hind legs to hips.

For the ear joints, I'll attach them to the head with a hinge role and tilt direction based on side, using explicit bone references since literal points lack bones by default. For eye placement I'll use decals positioned against the skull surface.

Writing eye SVG markup...

Switching to teardrop-shaped stain paths instead of gradients to avoid hard alpha cutoffs, then drafting the wrinkle lines as curved strokes across the viewBox...

Still writing SVG paths...

Still working out the bristle colouring, then shifting to the ear veins SVG -- mapping UV coordinates to pixel space and sketching branching vein lines radiating from the root attachment point toward the rim.

Checking vein endpoints against the ear outline edges...

I'm generating each vein as a quadratic path from root to tip with small twigs, wrapping the mirrored ear in a flipped group transform so the texture still reads correctly from the viewing side. Now I'm working out the plane's placement and thickness offset in the ear's local coordinate frame for the extrusion.

I'm checking how the plane geometry's normal and orientation should align with the ear's own axis, using a flat color material so the veins keep their own distinct coloring on top.

Checking that the vein's greyish-brown tone still counts as "colored" rather than neutral, since its channel spread passes the threshold. No whiskers needed, and I'm placing back-ridge bristle cards along the spine where the surface normal points upward, plus mud decals scattered on the lower flanks and legs using surface hit points.

For the decal placement, I'm working out how to position wrinkle decals at specific body heights and angles by using a center point at the right z-coordinate and sweeping azimuth around it to hit the correct side of the body surface. Working through the shoulder wrinkle placement now...

I also want small fold rings near the knees and elbows along each leg's chain — I'm figuring out the parametric t positions along the leg where the rings should sit and matching their radius to the leg's local thickness.

Still refining leg geometry...

For the tail I'm sweeping a tapering radius from the body out to the tip, then adding a hanging tuft ring at the tail end anchored to the correct joint bone so it bends naturally with the vertical frame orientation.

Next I'm scattering some bristle hairs near the base of the trunk, picking colors for the nails, mouth, dark skin creases, and tusk gums, then starting the module imports for the build.

Writing skeleton joint code...

Adding head and jaw joints...

Now I'm defining the trunk as a chain of catmull-rom points curving down and forward from the head, checking that the radius keeps the bottom clear of the ground, and adjusting the final points so the tip curls slightly upward instead of just dipping down.

I'm sweeping the trunk chain with a radius function that tapers to 0.1 at the tip and setting up a custom skin paint function that adds ridge detailing on top of the base skin color.

Now I'm setting up the tail chain from catmull points with default joint names, parented to the hips, then designing a leg generation function that handles both front and hind limbs with side-specific naming (L/R) to keep joint names unique, like "shoulderFL" versus "hipHL" for the knee and foot joints.

Writing the leg sweep and foot geometry...

Placing the nail boxes so they protrude slightly from the paw's curved surface, tying them to the foot bone, and adding an ankle fold ring around the lower leg for extra detail.

For the tusks, I'm attaching them to the head bone with a bezier sweep and defining a gum base cylinder oriented along the direction from the tusk base toward its first curve point, positioned near the muzzle at the front of the skull. I'm now laying out the skull assembly itself, starting with a sphere centered near the head's front-upper region.

I'm checking that eye decal placement will land correctly on the skull sphere's sides, and working out how the cheek bulge geometry overlaps with the eye position so the cheek's curvature pushes outward enough at that height to frame the eyes properly.

Still shaping jaw geometry...

I'll skip the mouth corner detail, but add brow ridges as small flattened spheres embedded onto the skull, then build eyelashes as a ring of tiny dark spikes around the eye socket.

Then I'm setting up forehead bristles as hair cards scattered across the skull and dome surfaces, filtered to upward-facing normals so they only appear on top.

Adding trunk and body bristle scatters, then defining the ear attachment point with its thickness, bevel, and outline smoothing, making sure the bottom tip stays sharp while checking for crossing points in the outline.

Now I'm positioning the ear root relative to the head's width and tilt, setting up the hinge joint for the ear part and working out how the extrusion origin aligns with the ear's outline.

Writing extrude parameters...

Working through the sign convention for the offset confirms z should be face*out*0.029, matching the plane's facing direction against the ear part's thickness axis. I'm checking that the plane orientation and texture mapping line up correctly with the ear's local coordinate system.

For the rim shading, I'm thinking of computing the thickness axis per ear as the cross product of its local x and y vectors, then darkening surfaces whose normal is roughly perpendicular to that thickness axis to simulate a rim effect. No poses seem necessary since the ears already rest in an extended position, and no glow effects are needed either. I'm now roughly tallying parts: one body, around eight head pieces, six ear segments, four eye decals, twelve lashes, and a handful of bristle cards.

Adding up legs at roughly fourteen parts each across four legs gets me to about fifty-six, plus tusks, tail, and trunk tori, landing near 120 parts total against a target of 180-340. To fill that out I'm adding more detail: extra toenail geometry, leg skin folds, a dozen trunk ring tori, wrinkle and mud decals, eyelids, temporal bumps, back ridge plates, belly folds, and scattered small flattened spheres across the body as skin warts to push the part count into the 150+ range while keeping triangle counts low.

Now I'm scattering these body bumps deterministically using a seeded rng function, then moving on to generate the SVG vein pattern for the ear—building paths from a root point out to several branch endpoints with quadratic curves and small twig offshoots, wrapped in a stroke group.

Writing twig offsets...

I'll skip the dashed inset outline idea and instead add a filled pink patch for mottling, since semi-transparent alpha patches won't render properly against the cutout.

Adding a second pink blotch for color variation, then considering how the decal API works for placing eyes onto the skull with target, texture, direction, and size parameters.

I need to check that the eye decal placement coordinates won't be overlapped by other overlying parts like the brow or cheek domes, verifying the y and z coordinates at specific azimuth angles stay clear of the skull surface geometry.

For the hit detection, I note the `.around(center).at(az, el)` method returns a nullable Hit, so I'll need to assert it's non-null when used. I'm also placing a mud stain decal below the eye socket at a steeper elevation angle with a taller, narrower size.

I'm generating a procedural SVG mud texture with scattered ellipses of varying size and two brownish color tones, keeping edges hard and fully opaque to look like dried dirt splatter, then moving on to think about body color variation.

I need to double-check the meta and default export setup, make sure foot nails attach correctly to the foot bone joint, and confirm the body part options support scale and flat flags alongside the skull's positioning. For the tail tuft, I'm placing a ring of small radius elements at the tail tip using a frame built from the endpoint and an up vector, making sure the ring's returned items are compatible with what cards expects, and that I'm explicitly binding the cards to the tail tip bone since frames built from raw points won't carry bone info automatically.

Now I'm writing a helper that builds a small torus "fold ring" with a square-ish tube using low radial segments, positioned and oriented using a chain point's axis. Writing fold ring helper...

I'm thinking through coloring these tori with a paint function that darkens the base skin color by mixing in a crack tone, then planning to loop across the trunk's chain points to place multiple tori scaled to the trunk radius at each step, oriented using each point's axis.

Now I'm shifting to body warts and bumps, using a stick helper with a small sphere embedded into the surface and squashed vertically, then moving into building the leg structure -- defining fore and hind leg roots and targets based on side, computing limb points between them with specific length and bend direction arrays, and checking that the total reach roughly matches the straight-line distance so the legs look nearly straight rather than overly bent.

Writing leg chain setup...

I also want to add rounded thigh and shoulder masses using extra spheres near the hip and shoulder joints to give the haunches a fuller, more natural silhouette.

Checking ground contact and overall proportions—foot bottom near zero, ear top around 3.53, back height near 3.3 all line up well with real African elephant scale. Now checking total body length including tusk extent.

Writing wrinkle decal helper...

Writing ear paint function...

I'm reconsidering the mouth placement — it would end up hidden near the jaw/trunk edge, so I'll skip adding that part. I'm also keeping the color palette minimal with just a few flat tones across the pieces.

For the tusk, I'm defining a tapered sweep with flat and pointed caps, worn tip detail, and checking that sweep/loft share compatible option shapes and radius function signatures for consistent typing.

I'm nailing down the limb bend parameters as number arrays, setting up a seeded RNG for card variation, and assigning colors for tufts and bristles before building out the foot geometry with a cylinder shape positioned near the leg target, watching for unused variable issues along the way.

Now I'm adding toenails positioned radially around the foot using sine and cosine offsets, then placing an ankle fold ring as a flattened torus, and chaining additional fold rings up the leg at increasing positions with slightly tapered radii to simulate joint creases.

I think the rig looks solid now, so I'm moving on to the eyelashes, using a ring helper attached to each eye with a callback returning the part, and double-checking that the SVG markup includes a proper viewBox before finalizing the answer.
